I found the paper you're looking for. Here's what the search revealed:

## Paper Overview

Causal-ACT is an extension to imitation learning models that integrates causal structure learning into a transformer-based policy model. The paper is titled "Improving Generalization Ability of Robotic Imitation Learning by Resolving Causal Confusion in Observations" and addresses how current imitation learning techniques can suffer from poor generalization, even under minor domain shifts.

## Key Innovation

The approach explicitly learns the causal relationship between observation components and expert actions by learning a causal structural function through intervention on the imitation learning policy. The method avoids reliance on disentangled representations and learns a causal structure model from standard convolutional encoders, jointly optimizing over a space of candidate graphs to find the appropriate structure that learns task-relevant features and avoids causal confusion.

## Experimental Validation

The approach was demonstrated using simulation of the ALOHA bimanual robot arms in Mujoco, showing that the method can considerably mitigate the generalization problem of existing complex imitation learning algorithms. The Causal-ACT method substantially outperforms the traditional ACT method under distribution shift conditions.

The paper was submitted on July 30, 2025, and is currently under review.

## SP-VLA: A Joint Model Scheduling and Token Pruning Approach for VLA Model Acceleration

SP-VLA is a unified framework that accelerates VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models by jointly scheduling models and pruning tokens.

### Key Components

The framework has two main mechanisms:

1. **Action-Aware Model Scheduling**: The approach designs an action-aware model scheduling mechanism that reduces temporal redundancy by dynamically switching between VLA model and a lightweight generator. It categorizes VLA actions into deliberative and intuitive, assigning the former to the VLA model and the latter to the lightweight generator, enabling frequency-adaptive execution through collaborative model scheduling.

2. **Spatio-Semantic Token Pruning**: The method mitigates spatial redundancy by designing a spatio-semantic dual-aware token pruning to preserve the most relevant visual information. It integrates edge and semantic information by extracting object contours using the Canny operator and estimating semantic importance via accumulated attention scores.

### Performance Results

The method achieves 1.5× lossless acceleration in LIBERO and 2.4× in SimplerEnv, with up to 6% average performance gain. Inference frequency and latency improve by 2.2× in SimplerEnv and 1.4× in LIBERO.

The paper appears on OpenReview for ICLR 2026 and is available on arXiv as paper 2506.12723, with code available on GitHub.

## Recent VLA Interpretability Research

A framework for interpreting and steering VLAs via their internal representations has been introduced, which projects feedforward activations within transformer layers onto the token embedding basis, identifying sparse semantic directions—such as speed and direction—that are causally linked to action selection.

VLAs can be steered via interpretable internal components by activating sparse, semantically meaningful neurons in FFN layers aligned with concepts like "up" and "slow" to modulate robot behavior at inference time, with experiments demonstrating that the method generalizes across models and tasks, influencing both simulated and real-world behavior.

## Visual Token Analysis in Vision-Language Models

Visual token representations become increasingly interpretable in the vocabulary space across layers, suggesting an alignment with textual tokens corresponding to image content.

Mainstream approaches typically adopt text-guided strategies, using text relevance scores to determine which visual tokens to retain, but this raises a critical question about whether visual and textual representations are truly well-aligned within LLM layers, with using text-guided strategies for visual token reduction introducing three forms of cross-modal misalignment.

## Causal Analysis Methods

Activation patching (also known as causal tracing or causal mediation analysis) is an interpretability technique for neural networks that selectively modifies internal activations while keeping others constant, allowing researchers to investigate how specific components contribute to model behavior and providing causal insights.

## Paper: Mechanistic Interpretability for Steering Vision-Language-Action Models (arXiv 2509.00328)

**Overview:**
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are a promising path to realizing generalist embodied agents that can quickly adapt to new tasks, modalities, and environments. The paper introduces the first framework for interpreting and steering VLAs via their internal representations, enabling direct intervention in model behavior at inference time.

**Key Methodology:**
The researchers project feedforward activations within transformer layers onto the token embedding basis, identifying sparse semantic directions - such as speed and direction - that are causally linked to action selection.

**Main Contribution:**
The paper introduces a general-purpose activation steering method that modulates behavior in real time, without fine-tuning, reward signals, or environment interaction.

**Evaluation:**
The method was evaluated on two recent open-source VLAs, Pi0 and OpenVLA, and demonstrated zero-shot behavioral control in simulation (LIBERO) and on a physical robot (UR5).

**Significance:**
This work demonstrates that interpretable components of embodied VLAs can be systematically harnessed for control - establishing a new paradigm for transparent and steerable foundation models in robotics.

The paper was published in August 2025 and has been accepted to the 9th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2025). A project website is available at https://vla-mech-interp.github.io/.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Shapley value token importance estimation for vision transformers:

## Overview

ViT-Shapley makes Shapley values practical for vision transformer (ViT) models by learning an amortized explainer model that generates explanations in a single forward pass. This addresses a key challenge in the field: Shapley values are a theoretically grounded model explanation approach, but their exponential computational cost makes them difficult to use with large deep learning models.

## Technical Approach

The work leverages an attention masking approach to evaluate ViTs with partial information, and then develops a procedure to generate Shapley value explanations via a separate, learned explainer model. The final explainer generates per-patch importance scores (196 values for a 14x14 patch grid) without the exponential cost of exact Shapley computation.

## Related Methods

FastSHAP learns a separate model (an explainer) to estimate Shapley values in a single forward pass, and it is trained by amortizing the WLS problem across many data examples. As a consequence of its WLS training objective, the globally optimal estimation model is a function that outputs exact Shapley values.

The research represents an important advancement in making Shapley-based explanations computationally feasible for complex deep learning architectures.

## ViT-Shapley: Learning to Estimate Shapley Values with Vision Transformers

The paper "Learning to Estimate Shapley Values with Vision Transformers" was published at ICLR 2023.

### Core Problem and Approach

Transformers have become a default architecture in computer vision, but understanding what drives their predictions remains a challenging problem, as current explanation approaches rely on attention values or input gradients, but these give a limited understanding of a model's dependencies. Shapley values offer a theoretically sound alternative, but their computational cost makes them impractical for large, high-dimensional models.

### Solution

The work aims to make Shapley values practical for vision transformers (ViTs) by leveraging an attention masking approach to evaluate ViTs with partial information, and then developing a procedure to generate Shapley value explanations via a separate, learned explainer model.

### Key Results

The approach provides more accurate explanations than any existing method for ViTs when compared against baseline methods like attention rollout, GradCAM, and LRP.

ViT-Shapley makes Shapley values practical for vision transformer models by learning an amortized explainer model that generates explanations in a single forward pass.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about RobustVLA (arxiv 2510.00037):

RobustVLA focuses on robustness in all modalities, and proposes RobustVLA against input and output noise perturbations, which delivers robust gains across 4 modalities and 2 backbones in both simulation and real-world settings.

The paper was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026 and addresses a key problem: existing methods target simple visual disturbances, overlooking the broader multi-modal perturbations that arise in actions, instructions, environments, and observations.

## Technical Approach

For output robustness, the method performs offline robust optimization against worst-case action noise that maximizes mismatch in flow matching objective. For robustness against VLA inputs, it ensures that the noise does not alter the semantics of the current state, so the optimal action remains invariant, and thus regularizes the objective to maintain consistent output actions across diverse input perturbations.

To account for multiple perturbations, the method formulates robustness as a multi-armed bandit problem and applies an upper confidence bound algorithm to automatically identify the most harmful noise.

## Results

On LIBERO, RobustVLA delivers absolute gains over baselines of 12.6% on the pi0 backbone and 10.4% on the OpenVLA backbone across all 17 perturbations, achieving 50.6x faster inference than existing visual-robust BYOVLA that requires external LLMs. Additionally, on the real-world FR5 robot, under four types of multimodal perturbations, RobustVLA shows strong low-data performance, outperforming pi0 by 65.6% success rate with 25 demonstrations.

## Test-Time Perturbation Learning with Delayed Feedback for Vision-Language-Action Models

The paper proposes Perturbation learning with Delayed Feedback (PDF), a verifier-free test-time adaptation framework that improves decision performance without fine-tuning the base model.

**The Problem:** Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) achieve remarkable performance in sequential decision-making but remain fragile to subtle environmental shifts. This brittleness is attributed to trajectory overfitting, where VLAs over-attend to the spurious correlation between actions and entities, then reproduce memorized action patterns.

**The Solution:** PDF mitigates the spurious correlation through uncertainty-based data augmentation and action voting, while an adaptive scheduler allocates augmentation budgets to balance performance and efficiency. Additionally, PDF learns a lightweight perturbation module that retrospectively adjusts action logits guided by delayed feedback, correcting overconfidence issues.

**Results:** On LIBERO robotic manipulation and Atari-57, PDF surpasses vanilla VLAs and VLAs with TTA baselines, improving decision performance with minimal overhead.

## Recent Work on Wasserstein DRO in Learning and Control

**Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF):**
A recent paper proposes Wasserstein distributionally robust regret optimization (DRRO) for RLHF, addressing the problem of reward misspecification. The work formulates RLHF under reward misspecification as an ex-ante DRRO problem and shows that Wasserstein ambiguity over reward functions reduces to deterministic ambiguity in their mean reward.

**Foundational Theory:**
Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization seeks data-driven decisions that perform well under the most adverse distribution within a certain Wasserstein distance from a nominal distribution constructed from the training samples. The optimal decisions can often be computed by solving tractable convex optimization problems, and they enjoy rigorous out-of-sample and asymptotic consistency guarantees.

**Reinforcement Learning and Imitation Learning:**
One framework proposes nonparametric policy optimization with Wasserstein constraints to control policy updates, deriving closed-form solutions using Lagrangian duality, and further improving sample efficiency by incorporating human guidance through imitation learning techniques.

**General DRO Applications:**
Distributionally robust optimization utilizing statistical distances has witnessed significant advancements, with comprehensive surveys covering both φ-divergences and Wasserstein metric methodologies.

The search results show active research in combining Wasserstein DRO with reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and robotics policy learning, particularly in 2024-2025.

## Key Approaches in Visual Token-Based Robot Learning

Recent frameworks integrate vision and action tokens driven by Mixture-of-Transformers architectures, with designs including shared latent spaces, closed-loop rollout mechanisms, and asynchronous inference pipelines for action prediction and motor execution.

## Causal World Modeling

Video world models provide the ability to "imagine" the near future by understanding the causality between actions and visual dynamics. Models capture the causal structure of physical interactions while enabling closed-loop control through continuous integration of real-world observations.

A compressive tokenizer discretizes video frames and an autoregressive transformer predicts subsequent tokens, allowing models to acquire knowledge of motions and interactions in various scenes through pre-training on diverse human and robotic manipulation videos.

## Handling Environment Invariance

Research shows that decoupling context from dynamics allows the model to focus on predicting the motion of objects while maintaining temporal consistency within the scene. Large-scale video pre-training helps models learn an accurate video prediction model which enables robots to understand what should happen in future steps, and this information guides action generation for trajectory rollouts.

## Intervention Mechanisms

Methods leverage KV Cache and causal masking to continuously update model memory with real-world observations, effectively transitioning the system to a closed-loop control mechanism and mitigating error accumulation in long-horizon tasks. At inference time, real observations are used as context, grounding the generation in the continuous observations of the physical environment.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about both VLA token pruning and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Here's what I found:

## LIBERO-Plus Robustness Evaluation

LIBERO-Plus performs a systematic vulnerability analysis by introducing controlled perturbations across seven dimensions: objects layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, light conditions, background textures and sensor noise.

The evaluation reveals significant robustness challenges:

- Models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations.

- Models are largely insensitive to language variations, with further experiments revealing that models tend to ignore language instructions completely.

- Models fail catastrophically when multiple perturbations occur simultaneously. The concept of Compositional Generalization Gap is introduced to quantitatively measure model performance under combined perturbations.

## VLA Token Pruning

For token pruning in VLA models, VLA-IAP (Visual Token Pruning via Interaction Alignment) achieves evaluations across three simulation benchmarks including LIBERO, reaching a state-of-the-art 97.8% success rate with 1.54× speedup without performance degradation compared to the unpruned baseline.

The method proposes an Interaction-Aligned Dynamic Strategy coupling spatiotemporal priors with an adaptive safety mechanism, using a Semantic-Motion IoU metric to assess interaction lock and dynamically switching between conservative and aggressive pruning modes.

content.content:
# Analysis of Token Pruning Research Findings

## Information Horizon Concept

The paper introduces the "information horizon" as a critical finding: visual tokens progressively lose salience through network layers, and beyond a certain depth, they become redundant. Specifically, the research shows that "the information of visual tokens gradually becomes uniform and eventually vanishes at an intermediate layer."

## Key Layer Findings

Three major discoveries about layer-specific pruning:

1. **Deeper layer degradation**: Existing pruning methods perform no better than random pruning in deeper layers (beyond the 20th layer)

2. **Variable horizon depth**: The information horizon's position depends on task type—it extends deeper for visually intensive tasks like OCR compared to general tasks like VQA

3. **Model capacity correlation**: Stronger VLLMs employ deeper visual tokens than weaker models, meaning the horizon "is also strongly correlated with model capacity"

## Evaluation Scope

The paper evaluates only **Vision Language Models (VLLMs)**, not VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models. The abstract and abstract details focus exclusively on VLLMs like Qwen2.5-VL and LLaVA-1.5.

## Scoring Recommendations

The paper recommends implementing "random pruning in deep layers" as an efficient approach. Rather than complex scoring methods, their conclusion supports using random pruning to "balance performance and efficiency" beyond the information horizon.

The paper introduces **Perturbation learning with Delayed Feedback (PDF)**, described as "a verifier-free test-time adaptation framework that improves decision performance without fine-tuning the base model."

The approach does **not** use causal intervention or token selection. Instead, it employs:
- Uncertainty-based data augmentation
- Action voting mechanisms
- An adaptive scheduler for allocating augmentation budgets
- A lightweight perturbation module that retrospectively adjusts action logits using delayed feedback

## Benchmarks and Main Results

**Evaluation Datasets:**
- LIBERO (robotic manipulation)
- Atari (video game environment)

**Key Results:**
- LIBERO: +7.4% success rate improvement
- Atari: +10.3 human normalized score improvement

## Addressing Spurious Correlations

The paper attributes model brittleness to "trajectory overfitting, where VLAs over-attend to the spurious correlation between actions and entities." PDF mitigates this through uncertainty-based augmentation and action voting, while the perturbation module specifically addresses "overconfidence issue" through delayed feedback-guided adjustments to action logits.

# Experimental Results: Causal-ACT vs Baselines

## Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Performance

The paper evaluates methods on a cube transfer task using the ALOHA bimanual robot in MuJoCo simulation. For the complete "transfer" task under OOD conditions:

- **ACT (baseline):** 0.23 success rate
- **Causal-ACT:** 0.82 success rate

This represents a dramatic improvement, with the proposed method recovering performance that had degraded substantially when test conditions removed distracting cubes present during training.

## Domain Randomization Comparison

Table 2 shows OOD transfer success rates with varying domain randomization parameters (k values):

- ACT + DR (k=+∞): 0.34
- ACT + DR (k=6): 0.48
- ACT + DR (k=3): 0.61
- ACT + DR (k=0): 0.91
- **Causal-ACT: 0.82**

Causal-ACT achieves performance competitive with the best DR variant while using less additional data and avoiding manual domain design overhead.

## In-Distribution Results

For completeness, in-distribution transfer success rates were:
- ACT: 0.89
- Causal-ACT: 0.96

The method uses a single task variant: picking up a cube and transferring it between robot arms, with position randomization within a 20cm×20cm area.

I found relevant information about GateFlow. Here's what the search revealed:

GateFlow is a paper submitted to ICLR 2026 that addresses how VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models may easily learn shortcuts by exploiting spurious correlations.

The paper proposes GateFlow as a method to mitigate shortcut learning in VLA models, where these models suffer from shortcut learning—exploiting spurious correlations between visual patterns and actions rather than developing semantic understanding.

The issue occurs because VLA models optimize an Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) proxy instead of the true likelihood, creating an optimization gap that enables memorized patterns to masquerade as genuine solutions. To mitigate this problem, the authors introduce GateFlow, a transport-guided gating mechanism that detects and suppresses shortcut learning by measuring the Wasserstein distance between observation and action features.

During training, GateFlow leverages ground truth actions to compute transport distances, providing direct supervision for the gating mechanism, while during inference, it employs iterative refinement where previous predictions serve as pseudo-targets, maintaining the same shortcut suppression principle.

The paper is currently under review and available on OpenReview at https://openreview.net/forum?id=qOSy2PX4xS.

## Overview

ViT-Shapley makes Shapley values practical for vision transformer (ViT) models by learning an amortized explainer model that generates explanations in a single forward pass. The work was published at ICLR 2023 as a notable top 25% paper.

## Problem and Solution

While transformers have become a default architecture in computer vision, understanding what drives their predictions is challenging. Current explanation approaches rely on attention values or input gradients, but these provide a limited view of a model's dependencies. Shapley values offer a theoretically sound alternative, but their computational cost makes them impractical for large, high-dimensional models.

The approach leverages an attention masking strategy to evaluate ViTs with partial information, and develops a procedure to generate Shapley value explanations via a separate, learned explainer model.

## Key Technical Details

The final explainer generates per-patch importance scores (196 values for a 14x14 patch grid) without the exponential cost of exact Shapley computation.

## Performance

The experiments compare Shapley values to many baseline methods (e.g., attention rollout, GradCAM, LRP), and the approach provides more accurate explanations than existing methods for ViTs.
